posts.hook: What I Learnt: New MCP 2.0 Release Today @ NY Event
posts.text:
MCP 2026-07-28 shipped today! I spent the evening at the New York release party for it in the New York Times Building at Datadog's office. There were three talks: Alexander Hancock (Block, Goose maintainer, keeps the official MCP Rust SDK) on the new spec, Scott Yak (Datadog) on what actually happens when you operate an MCP server at company scale, and Michael Levan (A fellow Agentic AI Foundation Ambassador) on the authorization gap. Let me tell you what I learnt!

No handshake state! What does that even mean?

Until today, MCP was stateful. You connected, your client/IDE initialized a handshake to negotiate protocol version and capabilities etc. and then got handed an Mcp-Session-Id, which got sent every request to the exact server instance which remembered you. The negotiation result got stored as a side effect of running the initialize call, and that side effect was the state.

The new spec deletes this whole ritual without any handshake or session header. This is kind of like how LLM providers use the stateless chat APIs (like we did at Bedrock too) -- You send your full request every single time. Every request now carries its own protocol version, client identity, and client capabilities, plus the method and tool name in HTTP headers (Mcp-Method, Mcp-Name) so a gateway can route it without even opening the body. Every request is self-describing, a complete little package, and any instance anywhere can pick it up cold.

posts.hook: Today the Model Context Protocol 2026-07-28 specification goes final, and the Python SDK v2 ships alongside it. Congratulations to the spec maintainers, the SEP authors, and the SD
posts.text:
Today the Model Context Protocol 2026-07-28 specification goes final, and the Python SDK v2 ships alongside it. Congratulations to the spec maintainers, the SEP authors, and the SDK teams - so much hard work was put into maturing the protocol as a whole, hard decisions were made, and SDK maintainers put in an epic marathon to get the SDKs in sync with the spec.

This is the biggest revision MCP has had. The highlights:

- The protocol core is now stateless. The initialize handshake and protocol-level sessions are gone. Every request carries its version, client info, and capabilities in _meta. Scaling remote servers just got much simpler.
- Server-initiated requests are replaced by Multi Round-Trip Requests (MRTR). A server that needs input returns an input_required result and the client retries with the answers, supporting statelessness.
- A new server/discover method, and caching hints on list results.
- The new extensions framework that allows for more robust and rapid development of new features outside of the release cadence of the core protocol.
- Tasks move out of core into an official extension.
- A formal deprecation policy. Roots, sampling, and logging are deprecated on a 12-month window, each with a clear migration path.
- Authorization hardening: OAuth 2.1 across the board, Client ID Metadata Documents replaces dynamic client registration.
 
The Python SDK v2 is a matching rework: MCPServer replaces FastMCP, fields are now snake_case, and context is injected explicitly. It also clears accumulated architectural debt, giving the SDK even better ergonomics. This is a breaking change, but mode='auto' keeps the two eras interoperating while you do it.

And guess who has the only book on MCP fully (or at least wicked close) up to date with the latest spec and Python SDK version? I'll drop the O'Reilly and Amazon links below.

#ModelContextProtocol #MCP #AIAgents

𝗠𝗖𝗣 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗱 𝗶𝘁𝘀 𝗯𝗶𝗴𝗴𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝘂𝗽𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗹𝗮𝘂𝗻𝗰𝗵.

The final 2026-07-28 spec is out today.
Here is what changed.

𝗤𝘂𝗶𝗰𝗸 𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗮𝗽: 
MCP is the interface that lets AI agents work directly with your software.
Whether it's Claude, ChatGPT, Mistral or one of the open models.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗶𝗴 𝗼𝗻𝗲: 
the protocol goes stateless.

Until now, servers had to remember every open session.
Clients were pinned to one server instance.

Gone.

Every request now carries everything it needs.
An MCP server deploys and scales like any other web service.

𝗔𝗹𝘀𝗼 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗿𝗲𝗹𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗲:

➡️ Extensions become first class: 
MCP Apps (interactive interfaces) and Tasks (long-running jobs) now evolve independently from the core.

➡️ Tool schemas support full JSON Schema:
Complex inputs and outputs without workarounds.

➡️ Authorization got hardened: 
six fixes for cleaner OAuth alignment. Your security team will notice.

➡️ Deprecated features (roots, sampling, logging) get 12-month transition windows. Evolution without breaking changes.

"We'll wait until MCP stabilizes."

I've heard that sentence a lot over the last months.

This release is that stabilization.
Your customers will expect their AI agents to work with your software.

The spec is ready.

Is your product?

posts.hook: MCP just went stateless! 💪
posts.text:
MCP just went stateless! 💪

This is easily one of the most important changes to the Model Context Protocol since its launch.

The new MCP specification removes the `initialize` handshake and protocol-level sessions.

In practical terms, MCP servers can now:

✅ Scale horizontally behind standard load balancers (I love this one :-D )
✅ Operate without sticky sessions
✅ Avoid shared session stores
✅ Handle each request independently
✅ Deploy more easily across containers and serverless infrastructure

And statelessness is only one part of the release.

Other interesting changes include:

• MCP Apps for interactive, server-rendered UIs
• Tasks for long-running operations
• Multi Round-Trip Requests for richer client-server interactions
• Authorization aligned more closely with OAuth and OpenID Connect
• A formal framework for protocol extensions
• A clearer deprecation policy
• Improved caching and infrastructure-level routing

This feels like MCP moving beyond its early experimentation phase and becoming a protocol designed for real-world, production-scale infrastructure.

There is a lot to unpack here—and probably quite a bit for MCP server and client implementations to update.

Full changelog:
https://lnkd.in/dy9tGTYs

#MCP #ModelContextProtocol #AI #AIAgents #DeveloperTools #Infrastructure #APIs

posts.headline: Product @ Stacklok | Built Carbon → acquired by Perplexity
posts.hook: I first came across MCP when it was announced...
posts.text:
I first came across MCP when it was announced in Nov 2024, shortly after Carbon was acquired by Perplexity.

My immediate reaction was: "Damn, I wish this had existed 8 months earlier."

At Carbon, we were working toward a similar vision: making it easier for AI applications to connect to the tools, data, and systems they needed. Despite its early limitations, MCP pointed toward a common, standardized protocol that could make those integrations far more universal.

Then, at Perplexity, I saw firsthand just how difficult it was to build connectors, maintain them, and deliver them reliably at scale without a shared protocol. Every integration introduced its own implementation details, operational burden, and ongoing maintenance. MCP offered a path toward making that entire surface easier to build, manage, and scale.

Now at Stacklok, I’m proud of the open source contributions we’ve made through ToolHive to help move the protocol forward, and to give platform teams the infrastructure they need to operationalize MCP securely and reliably at scale.

Today’s protocol release gives us even more conviction in where MCP is headed. It also reinforces that the work we’ve been doing around deployment, identity, authorization, observability, and governance is aligned with the broader direction of the community.

MCP is rapidly becoming the foundation for how enterprise agents access tools and data. The protocol is maturing, the direction is clear, and we’re excited to help turn it into infrastructure enterprises can actually trust and operate at scale.

posts.text:
Your company starts building an internal #MCPGateway. Soon, that gateway controls how every AI agent reaches internal tools and company data.  It works well, until one vendor's agent receives customer records from a restricted backend.

This was a session reuse attack. I found this in Agentic AI Foundation open source project agentgateway . Thanks to the solo.io team for fixing and preventing the issue quickly in v1.4.

The timing also matters because MCP gateways are moving into enterprise infrastructure. The official 2026 Model Context Protocol roadmap now treats gateway behavior, SSO, and audit capabilities as enterprise readiness work. Platforms such as MintMCP and JumpCloud are offering Gateway Control from different positions. The MCP today‘s 2026-07-28 release also moves the protocol toward a stateless core. 

An MCP gateway is becoming the identity and authorization boundary between agents and company data. Before we adopt it more broadly, one question is worth asking: Can your gateway verify the caller's identity, enforce the correct authorization policy, and isolate credentials across backends?

Jiquan Ngiam Christian Posta Chris Hughes

Full writeup and PoC in the comments. 👇

posts.text:
Today we shipped the largest revision to MCP since launch. What's in the 2026-07-28 spec release: 

- Stateless core: The initialize handshake and session IDs are gone. Remote MCP servers can now run behind a plain load balancer. You can deploy on serverless and edge infrastructure, or scale horizontally behind any load balancer.
- Extensions are first-class: MCP Apps and Tasks ship as the first two official extensions.
- Authorization hardening: We've aligned the spec with real-world OAuth 2.0 and OIDC deployments. While small on paper, this is big for anyone implementing clients or servers.
- Updated governance: A formal feature lifecycle, a conformance suite that gates proposals, and SDK tiers. 2026-07-28 and future revisions shouldn't require rewriting transport code.

Support for the new spec is rolling out across Claude products.
Learn more: https://lnkd.in/ggpGDhdc

If you're building with MCP, I want to hear from you. What are you working on?What are you most excited to build? What do you wish the protocol supported? Comment below.👇 Your input helps shape what we build next.

posts.text:
The AI ecosystem is moving incredibly fast, and one thing is becoming clear: MCP is evolving from a protocol into critical infrastructure for agentic AI.

Today I had the opportunity to attend the MCP Release Party hosted by Agentic AI Foundation AI Foundation (AAIF) and Datadog at The New York Times. It was an evening filled with insightful discussions, practical engineering lessons, and great conversations with builders across the AI community.

A huge thank you to Datadog and Agentic AI Foundation AI Foundation for organizing such a fantastic event, and to Angie Jones for keeping the energy high throughout the sessions.

### My biggest takeaways:

🔹 The next evolution of MCP explained by Alexander Hancock

* HTTP support alongside stdio opens the door for remote-first MCP servers.
* The move to a stateless protocol means every request carries the context needed making load balancing, scaling, and distributed deployments much more practical.
* Multi-round-trip requests (MRTR) allow servers to request additional information from clients when needed.
* Extensibility is improving through capabilities like long-running tasks and richer client-server interactions.
* One recommendation echoed repeatedly: use an official SDK whenever possible.

🔹 How Datadog is using MCP
Scott Yak shared real production use cases:

* Generating daily reports from server logs.
* Analyzing trends and automatically posting summaries to Slack.
* Running automated bug sweeps.
* Building a consolidated MCP server that exposes a common tool interface for multiple internal AI agents.

It's always exciting to see protocols move from demos into production systems.

🔹 Security will define successful agentic systems
Michael Levan gave one of my favorite talks of the evening, covering:

* Agent hijacking and prompt injection as emerging attack vectors.
* The growing importance of authorization and agent identity.
* Elicitation, where an MCP server pauses before executing sensitive tool calls and asks for human approval.
* Intelligent rate limiting not just for cost control, but as a way to detect abnormal agent behavior.

One thing I appreciated most was that the conversations weren't just about what MCP can do they focused on what it takes to build reliable, secure, production-ready agentic systems.

I met some incredibly smart people, had great conversations, and left with pages of notes. Looking forward to sharing more detailed insights over the coming days.

If you're building with MCP or working on agentic AI, I'd love to connect and learn what you're building.

posts.text:
🚀 MCP V2 just dropped — and I was in the room for the launch party.

Tonight I attended one of 7 simultaneous MCP release parties held worldwide — from Amsterdam to Austin, New York to London — with over 1,000 people gathering in person across all events. The one I attended was hosted by Manufact | mcp-use here in San Francisco, and it was a brilliant celebration of what is arguably the largest revision to the Model Context Protocol since its launch.

So what's new in MCP V2?

⚡ Massively increased throughput
🎨 Streamable UI (SubUI) — the first framework to support it natively
🦀 Faster Rust-based libraries with significantly improved cold launch times (huge for serverless/Lambda deployments)
📦 Smaller footprint — a tiny delta over the native SDK, but with all the plumbing built in: building, inspection, tunnelling, and full MCP renderer support out of the box
✅ Compatible with the new 2026-07-28 spec — the mcp-use team were first users of the spec and gave early feedback to shape it

The demo that stole the show? A fully voice-driven, multi-MCP-server orchestration demo using ChatGPT's voice mode — managing event attendees, ordering t-shirts, handling a waitlist, messaging via Slack, and filing expense reports to Notion. Zero keyboard. Pure voice. Multiple connected systems. It was a genuinely impressive look at where agentic workflows are heading.

Big thanks to Manufact and the mcp-use team for hosting. If you're building with MCP, the new spec and mcp-use V2 are worth your attention immediately. ⭐ the repo, check out the blog at https://lnkd.in/gnPM6xbV, and if you missed tonight — the education wave from the Agentic AI Foundation is just getting started.

Exciting times. 🤖

posts.hook: Amazing event yesterday, THE MCP RELEASE PARTY, at Datadog. Hugely valuable takeaways and analysis for everyone building with AI (addtl. resources in first comment). This MCP updat
posts.text:
Amazing event yesterday, THE MCP RELEASE PARTY, at Datadog. Hugely valuable takeaways and analysis for everyone building with AI (addtl. resources in first comment). This MCP update release represents the largest revision to the Model Context Protocol since launch. The release fixed the thing everyone building at scale was waiting for. It also made a quieter problem impossible to ignore. Three engineers, three talks, one arc:

Alexander Hancock (Block, maintainer of MCP's Rust SDK and the Goose agent) opened with the headline: "Statelessness — this is the big marquee change in this version." 
- In plain terms: every request now carries everything the server needs to answer it. "There is no initialize anymore. There is no session anymore." Before, a server had to remember your connection, like a barista holding your tab, which meant you couldn't freely cycle servers behind it. 
- Now any request can hit any server. Put a normal load balancer and an autoscaling pool in front, and it works. That is the infrastructure win, delivered on release day.

Then Scott Yak (Datadog) showed what that scale costs. Not in compute, in people. 
- Datadog's MCP server grew from 47 tools to 197 in months, across roughly 83 products. "Monolithic MCP servers don't scale organizationally." "The context is a shared commons": one team's bloated tool description taxes everyone else's.
- His fix is to let each team own its own server behind a single shared URL, so no one team is on call for 200 tools.

Michael Levan (solo.io) closed on the gap the spec still doesn't cover. "A new protocol, a new spec — that means there's going to be a new attack surface."
- The release added authorization improvements, but what an agent is allowed to actually do once it's authorized still isn't solved in the spec. 
- His argument: the MCP server is a black box you can't secure from the inside, so enforcement has to move one step earlier, to the gateway that every request passes through. That, he says, is where security gets implemented "nine point nine nine nine times out of ten."

The spec closed the scaling gap and opened the authorization gap in the same release. The infrastructure is now boring, in the best way. What an authorized agent may do next is the frontier.

Thanks to Angie Jones for hosting, and to Alex Hancock, Scott Yak, and Michael Levan for the talks. To Datadog for the room and Agentic AI Foundation for the series.

#MCP #AIAgents #AgenticAI #CloudSecurity

posts.text:
MCP graduation party was last night, sponsored by Arcade.dev, to celebrate the new MCP spec:
https://lnkd.in/gCF_HE-3

My takeaways:

From Alex Salazar: he almost made a competing standard for MCP purely to be a stateless alternative - so he's super pumped that MCP itself is now stateless. One standard to rule them all!
 
From Nate Barbettini, his migration guidance for MCP server developers:
* First of all, your servers won't instantly break if you haven't upgraded, as clients should speak both protocols for a while.
* But servers should expect to see "weird" traffic from clients, as MCP clients have been instructed to first attempt to use the new stateless protocol, and fallback to old stateful protocol if that doesn't work.
* If you were one of the 0.1% of servers that used roots, sampling, or logging, you should remove those now, since they're deprecated.
* If your server uses elicitations or tasks, you'll need to tweak your code for them.
* If you're using one of the official Tier 1 SDKs (or FastMCP), then they should support the new protocol out of the box, making upgrading easier.
* Once you think you've upgraded your server correctly, run the conformance suite! That's the only way to really verify.

From Sam Partee: MCP is rapidly becoming pervasive, so we need everyone to bring their diversity of perspectives to the table, so that MCP represents all your needs!

From Prathmesh Patel of MCPJam: 
* They just published https://caniuse.dev/ to help server developers figure out the matrix of client support for MCP features (like caniuse.com for web devs!)
* MCPJam now has a built-in XAA Debugger where you can use MCPJam as your identity provider, to confirm your XAA support works

From Leo Walker: AAIF now has an official MCP certification:
https://lnkd.in/gVAufb3S

Thank you Thierry Damiba for organizing, and for MCP cake!

posts.text:
Last night, I attended an amazing MCP event in San Francisco hosted by Arcade.dev and MCPJam. The occasion? The protocol got a huge new update that went live yesterday, and some of the leaders in the agentic space gave talks and showed demos about exactly what is changing and how to prepare for it.  Here are my main takeaways: 

- MCP is now a stateless protocol, removing the need for servers to maintain long-lived session identifiers and state info between client requests. Each request carries the information needed to process it, allowing for more 
scalability and a cleaner and more standardized mechanism of communication.

- MCP is moving more and more towards conformity and standardization as a protocol, both on the server and client side, which is a much needed change to reduce compatibility issues and inconsistency across integrations.    

- 𝗛𝗮𝗱 𝗹𝗼𝘁𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗖𝗿𝗼𝘀𝘀-𝗔𝗽𝗽 𝗔𝗰𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀 / 𝗘𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗽𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗲 𝗠𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗱 𝗔𝘂𝘁𝗵. People were very curious about this emerging use case, and it was exciting to be able to share that Descope is one of the early products that can act both as the OAuth authorization server and the ID-JAG validator. Descope can both issue and validate ID-JAG tokens, sitting on either just one or both sides of the equation, providing a lot of value in EMA scenarios. 

Thank you to the organizers and speakers, and thank you to everyone who I got a chance to speak to and network with; as always, learned a lot from y'all. And thanks to everyone who commented on the Descope "More Coffee Please" shirt 😅

posts.text:
Went to the MCP Release Party in NYC last night AAIF, with Datadog and Anthropic, at the New York Times Building.

One thing tied all three talks together: nobody was pitching what MCP can do. Everyone was talking about control.

Alexander Hancock on the new stateless spec, elicitation no longer needs an SSE stream held open and a server instance waiting in memory. State travels with the client in requestState, every request is self-contained, and you can finally scale a server horizontally without sticky routing.

Scott Yak on running the Datadog MCP Server - the context window is a shared commons, so every tool change is a potential regression for everything else in it. Vibe checks have to become real evals.

Michael Levan on the authorization gap - elicitation as a consent primitive. The server pauses before anything irreversible and asks a human, structured against a schema. "Scale payments-api to 0 replicas in prod?" is a question worth asking out loud.

Statelessness, evals, consent. All operational problems. That's what a protocol growing up looks like.

a MCP server used to hold the user on a long lived bi-directional socket. If a server restarted the tool run was killed. Now MCP servers can run behind load balancers or serverless functions 😬

posts.hook: Wednesday evening at AI House Amsterdam with...
posts.text:
Wednesday evening at AI House Amsterdam with our CTO Fernando Rejon Barrera, at one of the MCP release parties for the new spec; hosted by the Agentic AI Foundation, AI House Amsterdam and Prosus. Packed room, and for good reason.
Everyone's talking about MCP going stateless and I am too. Every request is now self-contained, no session pinned to whichever instance answered the handshake, no sticky routing, no shared session store. A plain load balancer is enough.
But the part we're most excited about at Zeta Alpha is the authorization overhaul. Three changes that matter the moment you deploy this inside a company:
Tokens are bound to the server they were issued for. A token minted for one MCP server can't be replayed against another; enforced by the protocol, not by application-level checks.
Anonymous client self-registration is on the way out. Dynamic Client Registration is deprecated; Client ID Metadata Documents take over. A client publishes its metadata at a stable HTTPS URL, and that URL is its identity. You can finally see who is connecting.
Enterprise-Managed Authorization is stable. Access decisions move into the IdP your IT team already runs. An admin approves a connector once, users inherit it through the groups and roles they already have, nobody gets a per-server consent screen, and there's one audit trail across every connector.
That last one is the real unlock for enterprise search. Connecting systems was never the hard part; proving who is allowed to see which document is. This puts that decision where it belongs.
We're building on both sides at Zeta Alpha: as a client, pulling secure customer knowledge cleanly into our platform; as a server, exposing Zeta Alpha's search, tools and agents so teams can use them inside their own workflows.
So: what are you most excited about in this release; the auth overhaul, the stateless core, Tasks, or MCP Apps? And if you're running many servers behind one agent, how are you keeping the tool surface under control?

posts.text:
Went to Agentic AI Night — the MCP Release Party this week, hosted by the Agentic AI Foundation along with Datadog, over at the The New York Times Building. Turns out this wasn't just a NYC thing either — it was part of a bigger series happening in cities all over the world, all tied to the latest MCP release.

Alexander Hancock, AI Agent at Block, kicked things off walking through the new spec and this shift toward a "stateless" architecture — honestly took me a minute to fully wrap my head around what that changes downstream. Then Scott Yak, Senior Software Engineer at Datadog, got into the messier, more honest side of things — what it's actually like running an MCP server in production, not just the shiny launch version of the story. And Michael Levan, AI Architect at solo.io, closed it out with a talk that stuck with me the most: "MCP and the Authorization Gap Nobody's Closing." Because everyone's racing to build agents, but almost nobody's talking about how exposed a lot of these setups still are.

If I'm being honest, that's the thing I keep thinking about since Tuesday — we're moving really fast on capability and comparatively slow on the guardrails.

But also, the best part of the night honestly wasn't only about the talks. It was also about getting to actually meet people — Matt, Levine, Ian Carter, Anusha, Mona and many others — and just talk shop for a bit. Feels good being in a room full of people who are all building towards the same thing.

Thanks to Alex, Scott, and Michael for the sharp talks and to AAIF and Datadog  for putting the night together.

posts.text:
The new version of the Model Context Protocol (2026-07-28) was released this week, and I am genuinely excited about it! 🚀

https://lnkd.in/epNaag7J

It feels like a big shift, and a shift in the right direction. The lifecycle becomes stateless: no more mandatory initialize handshake, no protocol-level sessions, requests carry what they need, and responses get real caching metadata. In other words, MCP is moving closer to how the rest of the internet is built: plain request/response, the way APIs and the web have worked for decades. That makes servers simpler to build, easier to scale, and friendlier to host behind ordinary infrastructure.

I was also lucky enough to attend the MCP Launch Party in London. It was great to hear the presentations, meet people building the ecosystem, exchange ideas... and, of course, enjoy the MCP launch cake! 🎂

Big kudos to everyone who made this release happen 👏
David Soria Parra Den Delimarsky Aaron Parecki Shaun Smith Peder Holdgaard Pedersen Radoslav Dimitrov Ola Hungerford Clifford Hall Marcelo Trylesinski and many others!

posts.hook: MCP is growing up
posts.text:
The 2026-07-28 release candidate makes MCP easier to run, reason about, and extend in agentic systems.

The next MCP specification release candidate is a big one. The headline change is that MCP is becoming stateless at the protocol layer, but the more useful story is what that does for people building agentic systems in practice.

A lot of protocol releases only matter if you’re deep in implementation details.

This one is different.

The 2026-07-28 MCP release candidate is worth paying attention to because it shows where the Model Context Protocol is heading. MCP started as a practical way to connect AI applications to tools, data, and services. That’s still the point. This release tightens the contract between clients and servers so those connections are easier to operate, observe, and evolve.

posts.author: Simon Willison
posts.hook: Stateless MCP has recaptured my interest
posts.text:
Tuesday was Stateless MCP day—the rollout of MCP 2.0, or the 2026-07-28 Model Context Protocol specification to use the more formal but less memorable name. This is the most significant change to the MCP spec since it first launched, and has also served to reignite my personal interest in the protocol.

For background: MCP is the Model Context Protocol, which describes a standard way to expose new tools to LLM-powered agent frameworks. It was introduced by Anthropic back in November 2024, had a huge spike of interest through much of 2025, and then became somewhat eclipsed by Skills (another Anthropic invention) when it became apparent that an agent harness with access to a terminal and curl could do most of what MCP did in a more flexible way. I wrote about that in my review of 2025.

I’m coming back around to MCP now. Giving an agent a shell environment with the ability to access the internet is fraught with risk, and requires a strong model that is capable of effectively driving such an environment. MCP tools are easier to audit and control, and simple enough that smaller models that run on a laptop can still drive them reasonably well.

The new stateless MCP specification also greatly decreases the complexity of implementing both clients and servers for the protocol. I built three of those this week!
